Endorsement: California hasn’t even bothered to study its existing public financing programs. No on Prop 4
Proposition 4 would overturn California’s ban on public financing of campaigns but does not include key guardrails.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 6, 2026
Americans don’t agree on much in today’s hyperpolarized climate. But they overwhelmingly believe that money is a corrupting influence in politics.
According to a 2023 Pew Research poll (https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2023/09/19/the-biggest-problems-and-greatest-strengths-of-the-u-s-political-system/), 85% of respondents said they thought the cost of mounting a campaign deters “good people” from running for office, and 84% said wealthy special interests and lobbyists exercise too much sway over politics.
Unfortunately, systemic reform to our campaign finance system is incredibly difficult. The 2010 U.S. Supreme Court decision in Citizens United struck down limits on independent political spending by corporations and labor unions.
But could California carve its own path to reducing money in politics?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
That’s what backers of Proposition 4 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf), which Democratic state lawmakers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) placed on the November ballot, contend their measure will do.
Prop 4 would overturn California’s ban on public campaign financing — in place since voters approved Prop 73 in 1988 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_73,_Funds_for_Election_Campaigns_Initiative_(June_1988)) — and give local and state governments the option of providing taxpayer funding for candidates’ political campaigns.
Supporters argue this will dilute the influence of special interests while making elected officials more accountable to voters — and leveling the playing field and encouraging more diverse, nonincumbent and first-time candidates.
That certainly sounds good, but is there meaningful research to back it up?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A natural place to look is California’s charter cities, which are exempt from the public financing ban; seven have programs (https://www.commoncause.org/california/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/CA-Municipal-Index-Reportv7-Final_Authored.pdf). San Francisco, Berkeley, Los Angeles, Sacramento and Long Beach provide matching funds to eligible candidates who receive a certain level of small-dollar donations; Oakland gives residents “democracy vouchers” they can donate to candidates and Richmond offers grants to candidates each time they reach a new fundraising tier.
How well have these programs been working?
Unfortunately, no one really knows. There hasn’t been much academic research into any of the programs, let alone a rigorous cross-comparison of them.
Despite a wealth of information on San Francisco’s public financing program — captured in an annual report from the city ethics commission — the data has yet to be thoroughly studied. Indeed, the overworked commission refers to its report as “primarily descriptive” (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2023/05/san-francisco-public-campaign-financing-program-report-november-8-2022-election.html) and practically begs for a “more comprehensive analysis” of the program — noting that (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2025/03/san-francisco-public-campaign-financing-program-report-for-the-november-5-2024-election.html) certain “labor-intensive” and “paperwork-heavy” aspects are “ineffective.”
Meanwhile, the studies that do exist suggest there’s a lot of room for improvement.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A 2013 examination of Oakland’s program (https://www.oaklandca.gov/files/assets/city/v/3/boards-amp-commissions/documents/pec/publications/reports-by-third-parties/2013-05-01-evaluating-oaklands-limited-public-financing-act.pdf) found “no evidence” that it reduced the influence of wealthy donors, spurred more candidates to run or increased voter turnout, although it appears to have made certain races more competitive and shrunk incumbents’ margin of victory. And a 2017 peer-reviewed study (https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/for-2017-0015/html) comparing New York City’s and Los Angeles’ public financing programs found that L.A.’s program design made it “substantially less effective” than New York’s.
All available research indicates that the effectiveness of a public campaign finance program depends enormously on how it’s designed.
Yet Prop 4 ignores best practices and imposes no meaningful checks on bad policies.
It gives local and state governments broad discretion to design programs, as long as they follow a few basic rules: To receive public funds, candidates would have to demonstrate “broad-based” community support — such as receiving a certain amount of small-dollar donations — and agree to abide by spending limits. They couldn’t use public funds earmarked for education, transportation and public safety — or use public money to repay personal loans to their campaign or cover legal defense fees.
“Cities are the laboratory of democracy … We wanted to give maximum freedom to jurisdictions,” Trent Lange, executive director of the California Clean Money Action Fund and co-chair of the Yes on Prop 4 campaign, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
But we’ve been running these experiments for years. The labs are in operation, but no one has bothered to gather the data or review the research.
And we have significant concerns about letting state and local governments run wild with taxpayer money — especially in the dark.
True, Prop 4 has some protections. The ban on using public funds to pay legal defense fees, for example, is aimed at closing the Eric Swalwell loophole: The disgraced Democratic ex-U.S. representative used hundreds of thousands of dollars from his California gubernatorial campaign (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/eric-swalwell-campaign-payments-22362761.php) to pay for his legal defense against multiple sexual-assault allegations.
But such protections are only meaningful if they’re enforced by independent, nonpartisan bodies. And Prop 4 offers no guarantee they will be.
In fact, it explicitly exempts the state’s respected campaign finance watchdog, the California Fair Political Practices Commission, from administering or enforcing local public financing programs.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Nor does the measure require local governments to set up their own watchdog agencies — even though Lange acknowledged “a public financing system needs a good oversight board.”
That’s a recipe for disaster.
Without San Francisco’s ethics commission, for example, 2024 mayoral candidate Mark Farrell — who received $1.2 million in public funds (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2026/03/campaign-finance-audit-report-mark-farrell-for-mayor-2024-id-1466726.html) — might have gotten away with illegally using funds (https://www.sfchronicle.com/election/article/mark-farrell-hit-ethics-fine-eve-of-mayor-election-19886013.php) from a separate ballot-measure campaign to subsidize his mayoral campaign (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/emilyhoeven/article/mark-farrell-campaign-finance-19654509.php).
We understand Prop 4 proponents’ hesitation to be overly prescriptive — San Francisco’s ridiculously clunky charter is the result of years of unnecessary regulations and stipulations being written into ballot measures.
But the details missing from Prop 4 aren’t ancillary. As the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office observed (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop4-110326.pdf), the measure leaves “many key design decisions” up to state and local lawmakers, who could directly benefit from the programs they create.
Consider the requirement that candidates abide by spending limits if they accept public funds. That sounds great, but Prop 4 doesn’t include guardrails for what a meaningful cap would be — and some local governments clearly need guardrails.
Thomas Hiltachk, a lawyer who frequently works on ballot measures and opposes Prop 4, cited the Los Angeles County city of Inglewood, which in 2020 capped local campaign contributions at the absurd amount of $100,000 per person (https://www.dailybreeze.com/2020/11/24/inglewood-caps-campaign-contributions-at-100000-to-avoid-new-state-law/) — 21 times the statewide max of $4,700.
This isn’t to say that public campaign financing is inherently a bad idea. We’ve supported the idea in the past (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Editorial-California-deserves-more-campaign-12165476.php), including a 2016 Berkeley pilot program (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Chronicle-recommends-Yes-on-Measure-X1-9984435.php).
But we can’t get behind a measure that doesn’t require local and state governments to adhere to any established best practices. This is a fatal flaw that opens the door to limited taxpayer funds being wasted on efforts that don’t meaningfully move the needle — at a time of widespread budget deficits.

candidates received an average of $1,284,158 in public funds.

Campaign finance is the raising and spending of money to influence
electoral campaigns at the federal, state, and local levels. While most
electoral campaigns are privately financed, 14 states and 26 localities
have implemented programs that offer public financing to candidates
running for certain state and local offices, such as governor, state
representative, mayor, or county council, as of 2024.1 At the federal level,
public financing of political campaigns is available to presidential
campaigns, but has not been widely used by major party candidates since
the 2008 election.
Supporters of public financing of political campaigns see these programs
as a way to increase competition, while reducing the influence of private
money in the political process and enabling candidates to spend more
time connecting with citizens rather than raising campaign funds.
Opponents of these programs believe that they restrict free speech
because they may limit the amount of money that candidates can spend
on political advertisements, and they may force taxpayers to subsidize
candidates whose views they may oppose.

The House committee report accompanying the Financial Services and

to revisit and update our 2010 report on public campaign financing
programs in two states, to account for data and experiences in selected
states and localities that have established systems of public financing
over the last five election cycles.2 This report addresses (1) key
characteristics of state and local public campaign financing programs in
five selected locations; (2) what available data indicate about the use of
these programs by candidates; and (3) factors affecting program structure
and candidate participation in public campaign financing programs, and
perspectives on the effects of these programs.
To address all three objectives, we selected public campaign financing

nongeneralizable case studies. These locations are Arizona; Minnesota;
the city of Los Angeles, California; Montgomery County, Maryland; and
the city of Seattle, Washington. To select these locations, we identified
programs that covered both executive and legislative offices, and had
been implemented for at least two of the last five election cycles at the

Campaign finance refers to the raising and spending of money to
influence electoral campaigns. Money raised for an electoral campaign is
also referred to as a campaign “donation” or “contribution,” and money
spent on a campaign is referred to as a campaign “expenditure.” Most
expenditures on elections are privately financed, via contributions from
individuals, political committees, and other organizations such as
corporations, unions, and tax-exempt organizations.6 In addition to these
private sources of funding, federal public campaign financing is available
for qualifying candidates for President of the United States during both
the primaries and the general election, and in states and localities that
have implemented their own public campaign financing programs.
States and localities that have implemented public campaign financing
programs have generally used three different models, according to our
review of relevant literature and interviews with representatives from
organizations familiar with these programs:
• Grants. The jurisdiction provides qualifying candidates with lump-sum
grants of public funds to finance their campaigns. The grant amount can
be either for the full or partial cost of a campaign, depending on the
program. In full grant systems, also called “clean elections” programs,
participating candidates may only make campaign expenditures with
public funds and may not raise private contributions after receipt of the
grant.
• Matching Funds. The jurisdiction matches certain private contributions
received by participating candidates with public funds at a set rate.
Depending on the jurisdiction, private contributions are matched either
dollar for dollar or at some multiple of public-to-private dollars. Generally,

• Vouchers. The jurisdiction provides eligible residents with a credit of
public funds (i.e., “vouchers”) to assign to one or more participating
candidates of their choosing. For example, all eligible jurisdiction
residents may receive four $25 vouchers, worth $100 in total, each
election year. Residents may then assign their vouchers to more than
one candidate or assign them all to the same candidate. Once residents
have assigned vouchers to participating candidates, the candidates can
redeem them with the jurisdiction for public funds to use in their
campaigns.
Selected public campaign financing programs have a range of
characteristics, which we identified as being associated with four key
categories. These four categories are (1) program goals, (2) program
funding and revenue sources, (3) candidate qualification and participation
requirements, and (4) oversight mechanisms to ensure program integrity.

Fast Facts
Most electoral campaigns are privately financed. But some states and localities offer programs through which candidates running for state or local offices can use public funds for their campaigns.
We reviewed 5 public financing programs. They all required candidates to collect a specific number of contributions to qualify and then adhere to spending limits.
The average amount of public funding that candidates received varied by office sought. For example, in the 2022 election, mayoral candidates in Los Angeles received about $1.3 million and city council candidates received $198,151.
The average amounts also varied by location.

Highlights
What GAO Found
States and localities have generally implemented public campaign financing programs using one of three models: (1) grants-participating candidates receive lump-sum grants of public funds; (2) matching funds-participating candidates receive public funds matching certain private contributions they raise, at a set rate; and (3) vouchers-eligible residents receive a credit of public funds they can assign to one or more participating candidates. GAO selected five programs representing the three model types (Arizona; Los Angeles, California; Minnesota; Montgomery County, Maryland; and Seattle, Washington) and examined their characteristics. For example, all five programs have requirements for candidates to qualify for the program, and once qualified, to receive public funds. These requirements include, for example, collecting a specific number of contributions to qualify and then adhering to spending limits to receive public funds.
Voting Booths
The amount of public funding participating candidates received varied by office sought and location, among other things. For example, in Minnesota in the 2022 election, legislative candidates received an average of $4,716 in public funds, and the one participating gubernatorial candidate received $584,034 in public funds. In Los Angeles in the 2022 election, participating city council candidates received an average of $198,151 in public funds, and participating mayoral candidates received an average of $1,284,158 in public funds.
GAO interviewed officials from the five selected programs and four additional programs (Albuquerque, New Mexico; Hawaii; Maine; and Washington, D.C.) to obtain perspectives on candidate participation. Officials from all nine programs said that many candidates are attracted to the public campaign financing programs because they provide an accessible source of funding. This may be particularly appealing for candidates with limited fundraising experience. Officials from eight of the nine programs said a key reason candidates may not participate is because they perceive the available public funding to be insufficient to run a competitive campaign.
Why GAO Did This Study
While most electoral campaigns are privately financed, 14 states and 26 localities offer programs through which candidates running for state or local offices can use public funds to finance their campaigns, according to a 2024 Brennan Center for Justice report.
The House committee report accompanying the Financial Services and General Government Appropriations Bill, 2023, includes a provision for GAO to revisit and update its 2010 report ( GAO-10-390 (https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-10-390) ) on public campaign financing programs. This report describes, among other things, (1) key characteristics of public campaign financing programs in selected states and localities; (2) what available data indicate about candidates' use of these programs; and (3) factors affecting candidate participation in these programs.
GAO selected five locations with state and local public campaign financing programs that covered executive and legislative offices, were implemented for at least two election cycles, and represented a mix of program models, among other factors. GAO reviewed relevant laws and documents and interviewed officials to describe key characteristics of the selected programs. GAO also analyzed candidate participation and campaign finance data for these five programs for the two most recent election cycles.
GAO interviewed officials from these five programs and four additional programs-selected using the same criteria-to obtain perspectives on public campaign financing programs. The findings from these interviews are not generalizable, but provide insight into state and local perspectives.

Fast Facts
Most electoral campaigns are privately financed. But some states and localities offer programs through which candidates running for state or local offices can use public funds for their campaigns.
We reviewed 5 public financing programs. They all required candidates to collect a specific number of contributions to qualify and then adhere to spending limits.
The average amount of public funding that candidates received varied by office sought. For example, in the 2022 election, mayoral candidates in Los Angeles received about $1.3 million and city council candidates received $198,151.
The average amounts also varied by location.

Highlights
What GAO Found
States and localities have generally implemented public campaign financing programs using one of three models: (1) grants-participating candidates receive lump-sum grants of public funds; (2) matching funds-participating candidates receive public funds matching certain private contributions they raise, at a set rate; and (3) vouchers-eligible residents receive a credit of public funds they can assign to one or more participating candidates. GAO selected five programs representing the three model types (Arizona; Los Angeles, California; Minnesota; Montgomery County, Maryland; and Seattle, Washington) and examined their characteristics. For example, all five programs have requirements for candidates to qualify for the program, and once qualified, to receive public funds. These requirements include, for example, collecting a specific number of contributions to qualify and then adhering to spending limits to receive public funds.
Voting Booths
The amount of public funding participating candidates received varied by office sought and location, among other things. For example, in Minnesota in the 2022 election, legislative candidates received an average of $4,716 in public funds, and the one participating gubernatorial candidate received $584,034 in public funds. In Los Angeles in the 2022 election, participating city council candidates received an average of $198,151 in public funds, and participating mayoral candidates received an average of $1,284,158 in public funds.
GAO interviewed officials from the five selected programs and four additional programs (Albuquerque, New Mexico; Hawaii; Maine; and Washington, D.C.) to obtain perspectives on candidate participation. Officials from all nine programs said that many candidates are attracted to the public campaign financing programs because they provide an accessible source of funding. This may be particularly appealing for candidates with limited fundraising experience. Officials from eight of the nine programs said a key reason candidates may not participate is because they perceive the available public funding to be insufficient to run a competitive campaign.
Why GAO Did This Study
While most electoral campaigns are privately financed, 14 states and 26 localities offer programs through which candidates running for state or local offices can use public funds to finance their campaigns, according to a 2024 Brennan Center for Justice report.
The House committee report accompanying the Financial Services and General Government Appropriations Bill, 2023, includes a provision for GAO to revisit and update its 2010 report ( GAO-10-390 (https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-10-390) ) on public campaign financing programs. This report describes, among other things, (1) key characteristics of public campaign financing programs in selected states and localities; (2) what available data indicate about candidates' use of these programs; and (3) factors affecting candidate participation in these programs.
GAO selected five locations with state and local public campaign financing programs that covered executive and legislative offices, were implemented for at least two election cycles, and represented a mix of program models, among other factors. GAO reviewed relevant laws and documents and interviewed officials to describe key characteristics of the selected programs. GAO also analyzed candidate participation and campaign finance data for these five programs for the two most recent election cycles.
GAO interviewed officials from these five programs and four additional programs-selected using the same criteria-to obtain perspectives on public campaign financing programs. The findings from these interviews are not generalizable, but provide insight into state and local perspectives.

Campaign finance is the raising and spending of money to influence
electoral campaigns at the federal, state, and local levels. While most
electoral campaigns are privately financed, 14 states and 26 localities
have implemented programs that offer public financing to candidates
running for certain state and local offices, such as governor, state
representative, mayor, or county council, as of 2024.1 At the federal level,
public financing of political campaigns is available to presidential
campaigns, but has not been widely used by major party candidates since
the 2008 election.
Supporters of public financing of political campaigns see these programs
as a way to increase competition, while reducing the influence of private
money in the political process and enabling candidates to spend more
time connecting with citizens rather than raising campaign funds.
Opponents of these programs believe that they restrict free speech
because they may limit the amount of money that candidates can spend
on political advertisements, and they may force taxpayers to subsidize
candidates whose views they may oppose.

The House committee report accompanying the Financial Services and
General Government Appropriations Bill, 2023, included a provision for us
to revisit and update our 2010 report on public campaign financing
programs in two states, to account for data and experiences in selected
states and localities that have established systems of public financing
over the last five election cycles.2 This report addresses (1) key
characteristics of state and local public campaign financing programs in
five selected locations; (2) what available data indicate about the use of
these programs by candidates; and (3) factors affecting program structure
and candidate participation in public campaign financing programs, and
perspectives on the effects of these programs.
To address all three objectives, we selected public campaign financing
programs in five locations—two states and three localities—to serve as
nongeneralizable case studies. These locations are Arizona; Minnesota;
the city of Los Angeles, California; Montgomery County, Maryland; and
the city of Seattle, Washington. To select these locations, we identified
programs that covered both executive and legislative offices, and had
been implemented for at least two of the last five election cycles at the
time of our analysis to ensure we could obtain similar information across
selected programs. We also selected these locations to represent a mix
of program models and populations, and considered information on
candidate program participation according to publicly available sources,
such as summary program statistics or annual reports found on a
jurisdiction’s website. For further information on the public campaign
financing programs in the five locations we selected for review, see
appendix II.
To address our first objective, we reviewed program documentation and
interviewed program officials to describe the key characteristics of the
selected programs in the five case study locations. To address our
second objective, we analyzed existing data from each of the five case
study locations obtained from program officials or public sources. We
analyzed available data on candidate participation in the public campaign

Campaign finance refers to the raising and spending of money to
influence electoral campaigns. Money raised for an electoral campaign is
also referred to as a campaign “donation” or “contribution,” and money
spent on a campaign is referred to as a campaign “expenditure.” Most
expenditures on elections are privately financed, via contributions from
individuals, political committees, and other organizations such as
corporations, unions, and tax-exempt organizations.6 In addition to these
private sources of funding, federal public campaign financing is available
for qualifying candidates for President of the United States during both
the primaries and the general election, and in states and localities that
have implemented their own public campaign financing programs.
States and localities that have implemented public campaign financing
programs have generally used three different models, according to our
review of relevant literature and interviews with representatives from
organizations familiar with these programs:
• Grants. The jurisdiction provides qualifying candidates with lump-sum
grants of public funds to finance their campaigns. The grant amount can
be either for the full or partial cost of a campaign, depending on the
program. In full grant systems, also called “clean elections” programs,
participating candidates may only make campaign expenditures with
public funds and may not raise private contributions after receipt of the
grant.
• Matching Funds. The jurisdiction matches certain private contributions
received by participating candidates with public funds at a set rate.
Depending on the jurisdiction, private contributions are matched either
dollar for dollar or at some multiple of public-to-private dollars. Generally,

these programs limit the size of contributions that are eligible for public
matching (e.g., $250 or less) and will not match contributions from certain
sources (e.g., government contractors).
• Vouchers. The jurisdiction provides eligible residents with a credit of
public funds (i.e., “vouchers”) to assign to one or more participating
candidates of their choosing. For example, all eligible jurisdiction
residents may receive four $25 vouchers, worth $100 in total, each
election year. Residents may then assign their vouchers to more than
one candidate or assign them all to the same candidate. Once residents
have assigned vouchers to participating candidates, the candidates can
redeem them with the jurisdiction for public funds to use in their
campaigns.
Selected public campaign financing programs have a range of
characteristics, which we identified as being associated with four key
categories. These four categories are (1) program goals, (2) program
funding and revenue sources, (3) candidate qualification and participation
requirements, and (4) oversight mechanisms to ensure program integrity.

Campaign finance is the raising and spending of money to influence
electoral campaigns at the federal, state, and local levels. While most
electoral campaigns are privately financed, 14 states and 26 localities
have implemented programs that offer public financing to candidates
running for certain state and local offices, such as governor, state
representative, mayor, or county council, as of 2024.1 At the federal level,
public financing of political campaigns is available to presidential
campaigns, but has not been widely used by major party candidates since
the 2008 election.
Supporters of public financing of political campaigns see these programs
as a way to increase competition, while reducing the influence of private
money in the political process and enabling candidates to spend more
time connecting with citizens rather than raising campaign funds.
Opponents of these programs believe that they restrict free speech
because they may limit the amount of money that candidates can spend
on political advertisements, and they may force taxpayers to subsidize
candidates whose views they may oppose.

Campaign finance refers to the raising and spending of money to
influence electoral campaigns. Money raised for an electoral campaign is
also referred to as a campaign “donation” or “contribution,” and money
spent on a campaign is referred to as a campaign “expenditure.” Most
expenditures on elections are privately financed, via contributions from
individuals, political committees, and other organizations such as
corporations, unions, and tax-exempt organizations.6 In addition to these
private sources of funding, federal public campaign financing is available
for qualifying candidates for President of the United States during both
the primaries and the general election, and in states and localities that
have implemented their own public campaign financing programs.
States and localities that have implemented public campaign financing
programs have generally used three different models, according to our
review of relevant literature and interviews with representatives from
organizations familiar with these programs:
• Grants. The jurisdiction provides qualifying candidates with lump-sum
grants of public funds to finance their campaigns. The grant amount can
be either for the full or partial cost of a campaign, depending on the
program. In full grant systems, also called “clean elections” programs,
participating candidates may only make campaign expenditures with
public funds and may not raise private contributions after receipt of the
grant.
• Matching Funds. The jurisdiction matches certain private contributions
received by participating candidates with public funds at a set rate.
Depending on the jurisdiction, private contributions are matched either
dollar for dollar or at some multiple of public-to-private dollars. Generally,

campaigns.

categories. These four categories are (1) program goals, (2) program
funding and revenue sources, (3) candidate qualification and participation
requirements, and (4) oversight mechanisms to ensure program integrity.

In summary
Prop. 4 would lift a ban that prohibits state and most local candidates from using public funding for their political campaigns. Proponents argue the mechanism helps more candidates run for office, but opponents are skeptical.

In 1988, a Democrat, a Republican and an independent in the state Legislature co-authored a ballot measure to ban most political campaigns from using public money.
Their rationale? There was already too much money in politics.
“It certainly makes no sense to open the biggest money source of all, the taxpayers’ purses and wallets,” proponents argued (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1988&context=ca_ballot_props). Nearly 60% of voters agreed.
Almost four decades later, some good-government groups argue that the state needs to do the exact opposite to counter the influence of money in politics.
They, along with the state Democratic Party, are backing Proposition 4 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-4-public-fundraising/) on the November ballot, which would lift the 1988 ban and authorize the state and most local governments to set up public campaign financing systems for state and local races.
Seven charter cities in California, including San Francisco, Berkeley and Oakland, were spared from the 1988 ban and already have public campaign financing.
To qualify for the funding, candidates must meet criteria such as proving they have a certain number of small donors or agreeing to cap how much they raise and spend on their campaign. Depending on the city, eligible candidates receive the funding as a grant, a matching fund indexed to their total donations, or a voucher voters can give to campaigns.
Proponents of Prop. 4 may face an uphill battle: Voters have twice rejected similar ballot measures to lift the ban, and public polling so far suggests voters are skeptical.
What supporters, opponents say
Elections have gotten more expensive over the past three decades, both federally and statewide.
In 2000, federal candidates, parties and special interests spent $5.6 billion on congressional and presidential races. By 2020, that number had nearly quadrupled to $18 billion (https://www.opensecrets.org/elections-overview/cost-of-election?display=T), according to OpenSecrets, a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit that tracks campaign spending nationwide.
In California, special interests spent $26 million (https://calmatters.org/politics/2025/10/prop50-money-ads-mailers-billboards/) running competing ads on redistricting last year, making it the most expensive ballot measure race in state history. This year, California had the most expensive governor’s race (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/03/us/elections/california-governor-campaign-finance.html) in U.S. history, with billionaire Tom Steyer pouring $213 million (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-rich-candidates-funding-elections/) of his own money into his unsuccessful gubernatorial bid.
Supporters of Prop. 4 say public campaign financing is necessary as a check against that kind of unfettered private campaign spending, because candidates often must accept campaign spending limits to qualify for public funding. They say public financing will lead to more diverse candidates by attracting those who otherwise couldn’t afford to run for office.

“We need to change the way we finance election campaigns so candidates can run and win without having to raise big money, and they can spend their time listening to voters rather than their donors,” said Trent Lange, president of California Clean Money Campaign and co-chair of the Yes on Prop. 4 campaign.
Gov. Gavin Newsom (https://calmatters.org/tag/gavin-newsom/) and the Democratic-led state Legislature, which voted last year (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb42) to place Prop. 4 on the November ballot, also support the measure. Sen. Tom Umberg (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/thomas-umberg-165043), a Santa Ana Democrat and a co-author of Prop. 4, said it would help alleviate a “growing cynicism in politics” and allow candidates to spend more time developing policies instead of fundraising.
“To the extent that we can engage particularly small donors, that will … empower and also engage the body politic, particularly young people,” he said.
But opponents say politicians should not use taxpayer dollars (https://caltax.org/prop4/) to run campaigns. They argue the measure would force voters to subsidize candidates they otherwise wouldn’t support, and that fraudulent candidates could exploit the system.
Voters have previously rejected ballot initiatives that would have allowed public money to be used for political campaigns. Nearly two-thirds of voters shot down a 2000 measure that would have allowed candidates to tap public funds for advertising (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2000/25_03_2000.html). In 2010, 58% of voters opposed a 2010 measure (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_15,_Biennial_Lobbyist_Fee_and_Public_Campaign_Funding_Measure_(June_2010)) to lift the 1988 ban.
“The voters have been quite clear they don’t want taxpayer money being used for politics,” Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican, said last year (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/278290#t=221&f=fe479f37ee7a3df6888379e9be069fd8) on the Assembly floor. “Unfortunately, politicians simply can’t take no for an answer.”

Critics also doubt the effectiveness of Prop. 4, arguing it is not specific enough to have teeth.
Prop. 4 offers only broad instructions to local governments and the state. It would ban candidates from using public funds meant for education, public safety and transportation. It would require candidates to prove they have enough public support and to agree to certain spending limits to receive funding, but doesn’t spell out how much. It would also ban candidates from using the money to pay for legal defenses, fines or personal loans to their campaigns.
The measure specifically exempts the Fair Political Practices Commission, the state’s campaign finance watchdog, from ensuring local programs are not exploited or abused, leaving it largely to local governments. But not every local government has its own watchdog agency, let alone an effective one.
The San Francisco Chronicle’s editorial board, in opposing Prop. 4, argued that its rules “are only meaningful if they’re enforced by independent, nonpartisan bodies. And Prop. 4 offers no guarantee they will be.”
Effectiveness debate
Fifteen states and Washington, D.C., offer some sort of statewide public financing for political campaigns, according to an analysis by the National Conference of State Legislatures (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/public-financing-of-campaigns-overview).
Studies are mixed on the effectiveness of those programs.
Some, including one in 2003 (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1532673X03256784) by two University of Maryland scholars, suggest that candidates who accept public financing spend less time fundraising, freeing them up for other campaign activities.
Some researchers found that public financing expanded the pool of candidates running for office. A 2022 study of Seattle’s program (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0047272722000780), which gives each registered voter four $25 vouchers to contribute to the campaign of their choice, concluded that the program boosted the number of candidates by 86%. Another study (https://web.stanford.edu/~neilm/The%20Impact%20of%20Public%20Financing%20on%20Electoral%20Competition.pdf) of Arizona and Maine’s programs found that they “significantly increased competition.”
Others disagreed. The United States Government Accountability Office, the nonpartisan research agency advising Congress, studied Arizona and Maine’s programs (https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-10-390.pdf) in 2010 and concluded there was no evidence that public financing led to more candidates.
There’s little evidence that public financing has curbed the influence of private donors, according to the Seattle study and the GAO report.
In California, few studies have examined the effectiveness of local programs. A 2023 San Francisco Ethics Commission study found candidates have increasingly tapped into the public funds and that third-party spending was “at near all-time lows.” But the commission encouraged a more comprehensive analysis. A 2013 study (https://www.oaklandca.gov/files/assets/city/v/3/boards-amp-commissions/documents/pec/publications/reports-by-third-parties/2013-05-01-evaluating-oaklands-limited-public-financing-act.pdf) in Oakland found no evidence its program diluted the influence of wealthy donors, although it did seem to boost competition.
Researchers point to the difficulty (https://sgp.jhu.edu/primers/public-funding-of-us-elections/#conclusion) of studying public financing programs, because most apply in only a handful of states and it is hard to measure what would have happened if the programs had not been in place.
The lack of compelling evidence makes Prop. 4 proponents’ claims shaky, the San Diego Union-Tribune’s editorial board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/09/04/endorsement-dont-buy-prop-4s-baloney-about-publicly-financed-campaigns/) argued.
“So Proposition 4’s only certain effect would be to create a new category of government spending that taxpayers could be required to pay for — one with no track record of delivering promised benefits,” it said.
The ballot measure should not be overly prescriptive, said Dora Rose, deputy director for the League of Women Voters of California, a co-sponsor of Prop. 4.
“Prop. 4 sets basic safeguards and then lets communities learn from the evidence and decide what works for them,” she said.
For now, voters appear skeptical. A September poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the Public Policy Institute of California found 53% of likely voters would oppose Prop. 4, while just 42% would vote yes. Another poll (https://escholarship.org/content/qt3w14s99c/qt3w14s99c.pdf) by the UC-Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies shows a tighter matchup, with 35% of likely voters supporting the measure and another 35% against it.

In summary
Prop. 4 would lift a ban that prohibits state and most local candidates from using public funding for their political campaigns. Proponents argue the mechanism helps more candidates run for office, but opponents are skeptical.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
In 1988, a Democrat, a Republican and an independent in the state Legislature co-authored a ballot measure to ban most political campaigns from using public money.
Their rationale? There was already too much money in politics.
“It certainly makes no sense to open the biggest money source of all, the taxpayers’ purses and wallets,” proponents argued (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1988&context=ca_ballot_props). Nearly 60% of voters agreed.
Almost four decades later, some good-government groups argue that the state needs to do the exact opposite to counter the influence of money in politics.
They, along with the state Democratic Party, are backing Proposition 4 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-4-public-fundraising/) on the November ballot, which would lift the 1988 ban and authorize the state and most local governments to set up public campaign financing systems for state and local races.
Seven charter cities in California, including San Francisco, Berkeley and Oakland, were spared from the 1988 ban and already have public campaign financing.
To qualify for the funding, candidates must meet criteria such as proving they have a certain number of small donors or agreeing to cap how much they raise and spend on their campaign. Depending on the city, eligible candidates receive the funding as a grant, a matching fund indexed to their total donations, or a voucher voters can give to campaigns.
Proponents of Prop. 4 may face an uphill battle: Voters have twice rejected similar ballot measures to lift the ban, and public polling so far suggests voters are skeptical.
What supporters, opponents say
Elections have gotten more expensive over the past three decades, both federally and statewide.
In 2000, federal candidates, parties and special interests spent $5.6 billion on congressional and presidential races. By 2020, that number had nearly quadrupled to $18 billion (https://www.opensecrets.org/elections-overview/cost-of-election?display=T), according to OpenSecrets, a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit that tracks campaign spending nationwide.
In California, special interests spent $26 million (https://calmatters.org/politics/2025/10/prop50-money-ads-mailers-billboards/) running competing ads on redistricting last year, making it the most expensive ballot measure race in state history. This year, California had the most expensive governor’s race (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/03/us/elections/california-governor-campaign-finance.html) in U.S. history, with billionaire Tom Steyer pouring $213 million (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-rich-candidates-funding-elections/) of his own money into his unsuccessful gubernatorial bid.
Supporters of Prop. 4 say public campaign financing is necessary as a check against that kind of unfettered private campaign spending, because candidates often must accept campaign spending limits to qualify for public funding. They say public financing will lead to more diverse candidates by attracting those who otherwise couldn’t afford to run for office.

“We need to change the way we finance election campaigns so candidates can run and win without having to raise big money, and they can spend their time listening to voters rather than their donors,” said Trent Lange, president of California Clean Money Campaign and co-chair of the Yes on Prop. 4 campaign.
Gov. Gavin Newsom (https://calmatters.org/tag/gavin-newsom/) and the Democratic-led state Legislature, which voted last year (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb42) to place Prop. 4 on the November ballot, also support the measure. Sen. Tom Umberg (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/thomas-umberg-165043), a Santa Ana Democrat and a co-author of Prop. 4, said it would help alleviate a “growing cynicism in politics” and allow candidates to spend more time developing policies instead of fundraising.
“To the extent that we can engage particularly small donors, that will … empower and also engage the body politic, particularly young people,” he said.
But opponents say politicians should not use taxpayer dollars (https://caltax.org/prop4/) to run campaigns. They argue the measure would force voters to subsidize candidates they otherwise wouldn’t support, and that fraudulent candidates could exploit the system.
Voters have previously rejected ballot initiatives that would have allowed public money to be used for political campaigns. Nearly two-thirds of voters shot down a 2000 measure that would have allowed candidates to tap public funds for advertising (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2000/25_03_2000.html). In 2010, 58% of voters opposed a 2010 measure (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_15,_Biennial_Lobbyist_Fee_and_Public_Campaign_Funding_Measure_(June_2010)) to lift the 1988 ban.
“The voters have been quite clear they don’t want taxpayer money being used for politics,” Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican, said last year (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/278290#t=221&f=fe479f37ee7a3df6888379e9be069fd8) on the Assembly floor. “Unfortunately, politicians simply can’t take no for an answer.”

Critics also doubt the effectiveness of Prop. 4, arguing it is not specific enough to have teeth.
Prop. 4 offers only broad instructions to local governments and the state. It would ban candidates from using public funds meant for education, public safety and transportation. It would require candidates to prove they have enough public support and to agree to certain spending limits to receive funding, but doesn’t spell out how much. It would also ban candidates from using the money to pay for legal defenses, fines or personal loans to their campaigns.
The measure specifically exempts the Fair Political Practices Commission, the state’s campaign finance watchdog, from ensuring local programs are not exploited or abused, leaving it largely to local governments. But not every local government has its own watchdog agency, let alone an effective one.
The San Francisco Chronicle’s editorial board, in opposing Prop. 4, argued that its rules “are only meaningful if they’re enforced by independent, nonpartisan bodies. And Prop. 4 offers no guarantee they will be.”
Effectiveness debate
Fifteen states and Washington, D.C., offer some sort of statewide public financing for political campaigns, according to an analysis by the National Conference of State Legislatures (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/public-financing-of-campaigns-overview).
Studies are mixed on the effectiveness of those programs.
Some, including one in 2003 (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1532673X03256784) by two University of Maryland scholars, suggest that candidates who accept public financing spend less time fundraising, freeing them up for other campaign activities.
Some researchers found that public financing expanded the pool of candidates running for office. A 2022 study of Seattle’s program (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0047272722000780), which gives each registered voter four $25 vouchers to contribute to the campaign of their choice, concluded that the program boosted the number of candidates by 86%. Another study (https://web.stanford.edu/~neilm/The%20Impact%20of%20Public%20Financing%20on%20Electoral%20Competition.pdf) of Arizona and Maine’s programs found that they “significantly increased competition.”
Others disagreed. The United States Government Accountability Office, the nonpartisan research agency advising Congress, studied Arizona and Maine’s programs (https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-10-390.pdf) in 2010 and concluded there was no evidence that public financing led to more candidates.
There’s little evidence that public financing has curbed the influence of private donors, according to the Seattle study and the GAO report.
In California, few studies have examined the effectiveness of local programs. A 2023 San Francisco Ethics Commission study found candidates have increasingly tapped into the public funds and that third-party spending was “at near all-time lows.” But the commission encouraged a more comprehensive analysis. A 2013 study (https://www.oaklandca.gov/files/assets/city/v/3/boards-amp-commissions/documents/pec/publications/reports-by-third-parties/2013-05-01-evaluating-oaklands-limited-public-financing-act.pdf) in Oakland found no evidence its program diluted the influence of wealthy donors, although it did seem to boost competition.
Researchers point to the difficulty (https://sgp.jhu.edu/primers/public-funding-of-us-elections/#conclusion) of studying public financing programs, because most apply in only a handful of states and it is hard to measure what would have happened if the programs had not been in place.
The lack of compelling evidence makes Prop. 4 proponents’ claims shaky, the San Diego Union-Tribune’s editorial board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/09/04/endorsement-dont-buy-prop-4s-baloney-about-publicly-financed-campaigns/) argued.
“So Proposition 4’s only certain effect would be to create a new category of government spending that taxpayers could be required to pay for — one with no track record of delivering promised benefits,” it said.
The ballot measure should not be overly prescriptive, said Dora Rose, deputy director for the League of Women Voters of California, a co-sponsor of Prop. 4.
“Prop. 4 sets basic safeguards and then lets communities learn from the evidence and decide what works for them,” she said.
For now, voters appear skeptical. A September poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the Public Policy Institute of California found 53% of likely voters would oppose Prop. 4, while just 42% would vote yes. Another poll (https://escholarship.org/content/qt3w14s99c/qt3w14s99c.pdf) by the UC-Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies shows a tighter matchup, with 35% of likely voters supporting the measure and another 35% against it.

Americans don’t agree on much in today’s hyperpolarized climate. But they overwhelmingly believe that money is a corrupting influence in politics.
According to a 2023 Pew Research poll (https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2023/09/19/the-biggest-problems-and-greatest-strengths-of-the-u-s-political-system/), 85% of respondents said they thought the cost of mounting a campaign deters “good people” from running for office, and 84% said wealthy special interests and lobbyists exercise too much sway over politics.
Unfortunately, systemic reform to our campaign finance system is incredibly difficult. The 2010 U.S. Supreme Court decision in Citizens United struck down limits on independent political spending by corporations and labor unions.
But could California carve its own path to reducing money in politics?

There is little evidence in California and across the nation that public financing of candidates has had the broadly beneficial effects that advocates predicted. (SCNG)
By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 4, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: September 10, 2026 at 10:32 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Few political beliefs are as fervently held as the view that public financing of candidates would quickly improve their quality and variety, reduce the clout of “special interests,” and promote both public trust and better government.
This is why Californians will be asked in November to enact Proposition 4 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_4,_Allow_Public_Financing_of_Election_Campaigns_Measure_(2026)), which would overturn the voter-approved 1988 law that prohibits state and local governments from using taxpayer money to provide campaign funding to candidates.
The state Legislature placed the measure on the ballot after being urged to do so (https://laist.com/news/politics/public-funding-for-elections-the-idea-is-back-in-california-fair-elections-act-ben-allen) by groups such as the League of Women Voters, which argues that public financing “helps engage unrepresented communities in the political process” and “makes our democracy ultimately much stronger.”
But most claims made by advocates don’t hold up. There is no empirical evidence that shows public financing of candidates improves governance.
In California, charter cities are allowed to provide public financing. All five that have done so — Los Angeles, Long Beach, San Francisco, Oakland and Berkeley — are considered poorly run. They’re dominated by government unions, by far the Golden State’s most powerful special interest.
Meanwhile, most of the 14 states that allow for public financing have programs that are little-used or practically defunct. Those with higher participation (such as Arizona, Minnesota and New York) usually show modest increases (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/state-politics-and-policy-quarterly/article/does-public-financing-motivate-electoral-challengers/6365D1FA24C0A905E69A899B678909C5) in candidate diversity. They also undercut claims that public financing will lead to a flood of unqualified candidates who are eager to use taxpayer funds to spread their views.
But whether in California or these states, there is no evidence that public financing has led to different policy outcomes or increased public trust.
Defenders of the reform will say that’s because there’s so much private financing — i.e., special interest money — in elections. But that’s not going to change. The Supreme Court has repeatedly made clear that paid political speech is constitutionally protected free speech.
So Proposition 4’s only certain effect would be to create a new category of government spending that taxpayers could be required to pay for — one with no track record of delivering promised benefits. Even if California wasn’t in an era of tight local and state budgets, this measure would deserve to be rejected.
The final paragraph has been revised to more precisely describe Proposition 4's effects if approved. It would not automatically require more government spending. State and local lawmakers would need to approve public financing of candidate campaigns for that to happen.

There is little evidence in California and across the nation that public financing of candidates has had the broadly beneficial effects that advocates predicted. (SCNG)
By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 4, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: September 10, 2026 at 10:32 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Few political beliefs are as fervently held as the view that public financing of candidates would quickly improve their quality and variety, reduce the clout of “special interests,” and promote both public trust and better government.
This is why Californians will be asked in November to enact Proposition 4 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_4,_Allow_Public_Financing_of_Election_Campaigns_Measure_(2026)), which would overturn the voter-approved 1988 law that prohibits state and local governments from using taxpayer money to provide campaign funding to candidates.
The state Legislature placed the measure on the ballot after being urged to do so (https://laist.com/news/politics/public-funding-for-elections-the-idea-is-back-in-california-fair-elections-act-ben-allen) by groups such as the League of Women Voters, which argues that public financing “helps engage unrepresented communities in the political process” and “makes our democracy ultimately much stronger.”
But most claims made by advocates don’t hold up. There is no empirical evidence that shows public financing of candidates improves governance.
In California, charter cities are allowed to provide public financing. All five that have done so — Los Angeles, Long Beach, San Francisco, Oakland and Berkeley — are considered poorly run. They’re dominated by government unions, by far the Golden State’s most powerful special interest.
Meanwhile, most of the 14 states that allow for public financing have programs that are little-used or practically defunct. Those with higher participation (such as Arizona, Minnesota and New York) usually show modest increases (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/state-politics-and-policy-quarterly/article/does-public-financing-motivate-electoral-challengers/6365D1FA24C0A905E69A899B678909C5) in candidate diversity. They also undercut claims that public financing will lead to a flood of unqualified candidates who are eager to use taxpayer funds to spread their views.
But whether in California or these states, there is no evidence that public financing has led to different policy outcomes or increased public trust.
Defenders of the reform will say that’s because there’s so much private financing — i.e., special interest money — in elections. But that’s not going to change. The Supreme Court has repeatedly made clear that paid political speech is constitutionally protected free speech.
So Proposition 4’s only certain effect would be to create a new category of government spending that taxpayers could be required to pay for — one with no track record of delivering promised benefits. Even if California wasn’t in an era of tight local and state budgets, this measure would deserve to be rejected.
The final paragraph has been revised to more precisely describe Proposition 4's effects if approved. It would not automatically require more government spending. State and local lawmakers would need to approve public financing of candidate campaigns for that to happen.

How to vote on California’s Proposition 4: McClatchy Media’s recommendation | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial boards
Updated October 2, 2026 4:49 PM
"I voted" stickers await voters at the Placer County Clerk-Recorder-Elections Office in Rocklin on Tuesday, Oct. 28, 2025. Proposition 4 would repeal California’s ban on public financing of political campaigns.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
Of the 14 propositions on California’s November ballot, Proposition 4 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317016880.html) could be one of the least accessible to the average voter.
Here is what you need to know: A “Yes” vote on Prop. 4 would repeal a more than 30-year ban on the use of tax dollars to fund local and state elections.
“The measure (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=4&year=2026) would allow state and local governments to create programs for the use of certain public funds to finance political campaigns,” wrote The Bee last week. “Candidates would be prohibited from using the funds to repay personal loans to their campaigns, legal defense fees or fines. Those who receive public funds would be required to show broad-based local support and pledge their compliance with spending limits and other rules.”
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 4 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317016880.html)
Public money set aside for education, transportation or public safety would not be available to be used for local and state elections. “Public funds cannot be used for legal defense fees or fines, or to repay a candidate’s personal campaign loan,” wrote the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
“We just want to lift the ban, putting into place certain reasonable, common-sense taxpayer requirements so that communities have the opportunity to use public financing to allow qualified candidates the chance to run,” said Trent Lange, president and executive director of the California Clean Money Campaign.
Other groups in favor of Prop. 4 include the California Democratic Party, ACLU California Action (https://aclucalaction.org/2026-election-guide/), California Clean Money Action Fund, End Citizens United and the League of Women Voters of California, as well as state senators Ben Allen, D-Santa Monica; Sabrina Cervantes, D-Riverside; and Tom Umberg, D-Villa Park. Those in opposition are the California Republican Party, Reform California and California Taxpayers Association.
The editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/), Modesto Bee, (https://www.modbee.com/)Merced Sun-Star (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/), Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) recommend a “Yes” vote on Prop. 4. The measure would end the state’s overly restrictive ban on public financing of campaigns. Public financing amplifies the voices of everyday voters and gives candidates an alternative to relying on wealthy donors.
A “Yes” vote would allow local governments to create matching-fund programs, in which public money matches small private donations, or public campaign-grant programs that provide qualifying candidates with a set amount of taxpayer money. Such programs would reduce candidates’ dependence on large donors and political committees, lower barriers to running for office, and help build a more diverse and representative democracy.
“Everybody knows that the amount of money in politics is outrageous, and it’s corrupting our democracy,” Lange told the board.
“All that money buys access for special interests while shutting out the rest of us. We believe that we need to change the way we finance election campaigns so that elected officials can focus on working for the people, rather than their big-money donors.”

How to vote on California’s Proposition 4: McClatchy Media’s recommendation | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial boards
Updated October 2, 2026 4:49 PM
"I voted" stickers await voters at the Placer County Clerk-Recorder-Elections Office in Rocklin on Tuesday, Oct. 28, 2025. Proposition 4 would repeal California’s ban on public financing of political campaigns.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
Of the 14 propositions on California’s November ballot, Proposition 4 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317016880.html) could be one of the least accessible to the average voter.
Here is what you need to know: A “Yes” vote on Prop. 4 would repeal a more than 30-year ban on the use of tax dollars to fund local and state elections.
“The measure (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=4&year=2026) would allow state and local governments to create programs for the use of certain public funds to finance political campaigns,” wrote The Bee last week. “Candidates would be prohibited from using the funds to repay personal loans to their campaigns, legal defense fees or fines. Those who receive public funds would be required to show broad-based local support and pledge their compliance with spending limits and other rules.”
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 4 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317016880.html)
Public money set aside for education, transportation or public safety would not be available to be used for local and state elections. “Public funds cannot be used for legal defense fees or fines, or to repay a candidate’s personal campaign loan,” wrote the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
“We just want to lift the ban, putting into place certain reasonable, common-sense taxpayer requirements so that communities have the opportunity to use public financing to allow qualified candidates the chance to run,” said Trent Lange, president and executive director of the California Clean Money Campaign.
Other groups in favor of Prop. 4 include the California Democratic Party, ACLU California Action (https://aclucalaction.org/2026-election-guide/), California Clean Money Action Fund, End Citizens United and the League of Women Voters of California, as well as state senators Ben Allen, D-Santa Monica; Sabrina Cervantes, D-Riverside; and Tom Umberg, D-Villa Park. Those in opposition are the California Republican Party, Reform California and California Taxpayers Association.
The editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/), Modesto Bee, (https://www.modbee.com/)Merced Sun-Star (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/), Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) recommend a “Yes” vote on Prop. 4. The measure would end the state’s overly restrictive ban on public financing of campaigns. Public financing amplifies the voices of everyday voters and gives candidates an alternative to relying on wealthy donors.
A “Yes” vote would allow local governments to create matching-fund programs, in which public money matches small private donations, or public campaign-grant programs that provide qualifying candidates with a set amount of taxpayer money. Such programs would reduce candidates’ dependence on large donors and political committees, lower barriers to running for office, and help build a more diverse and representative democracy.
“Everybody knows that the amount of money in politics is outrageous, and it’s corrupting our democracy,” Lange told the board.
“All that money buys access for special interests while shutting out the rest of us. We believe that we need to change the way we finance election campaigns so that elected officials can focus on working for the people, rather than their big-money donors.”

Fast Facts
Most electoral campaigns are privately financed. But some states and localities offer programs through which candidates running for state or local offices can use public funds for their campaigns.
We reviewed 5 public financing programs. They all required candidates to collect a specific number of contributions to qualify and then adhere to spending limits.
The average amount of public funding that candidates received varied by office sought. For example, in the 2022 election, mayoral candidates in Los Angeles received about $1.3 million and city council candidates received $198,151.
The average amounts also varied by location.
Skip to Highlights
Highlights
What GAO Found
States and localities have generally implemented public campaign financing programs using one of three models: (1) grants-participating candidates receive lump-sum grants of public funds; (2) matching funds-participating candidates receive public funds matching certain private contributions they raise, at a set rate; and (3) vouchers-eligible residents receive a credit of public funds they can assign to one or more participating candidates. GAO selected five programs representing the three model types (Arizona; Los Angeles, California; Minnesota; Montgomery County, Maryland; and Seattle, Washington) and examined their characteristics. For example, all five programs have requirements for candidates to qualify for the program, and once qualified, to receive public funds. These requirements include, for example, collecting a specific number of contributions to qualify and then adhering to spending limits to receive public funds.
Voting Booths
The amount of public funding participating candidates received varied by office sought and location, among other things. For example, in Minnesota in the 2022 election, legislative candidates received an average of $4,716 in public funds, and the one participating gubernatorial candidate received $584,034 in public funds. In Los Angeles in the 2022 election, participating city council candidates received an average of $198,151 in public funds, and participating mayoral candidates received an average of $1,284,158 in public funds.
GAO interviewed officials from the five selected programs and four additional programs (Albuquerque, New Mexico; Hawaii; Maine; and Washington, D.C.) to obtain perspectives on candidate participation. Officials from all nine programs said that many candidates are attracted to the public campaign financing programs because they provide an accessible source of funding. This may be particularly appealing for candidates with limited fundraising experience. Officials from eight of the nine programs said a key reason candidates may not participate is because they perceive the available public funding to be insufficient to run a competitive campaign.
Why GAO Did This Study
While most electoral campaigns are privately financed, 14 states and 26 localities offer programs through which candidates running for state or local offices can use public funds to finance their campaigns, according to a 2024 Brennan Center for Justice report.
The House committee report accompanying the Financial Services and General Government Appropriations Bill, 2023, includes a provision for GAO to revisit and update its 2010 report ( GAO-10-390 (https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-10-390) ) on public campaign financing programs. This report describes, among other things, (1) key characteristics of public campaign financing programs in selected states and localities; (2) what available data indicate about candidates' use of these programs; and (3) factors affecting candidate participation in these programs.
GAO selected five locations with state and local public campaign financing programs that covered executive and legislative offices, were implemented for at least two election cycles, and represented a mix of program models, among other factors. GAO reviewed relevant laws and documents and interviewed officials to describe key characteristics of the selected programs. GAO also analyzed candidate participation and campaign finance data for these five programs for the two most recent election cycles.
GAO interviewed officials from these five programs and four additional programs-selected using the same criteria-to obtain perspectives on public campaign financing programs. The findings from these interviews are not generalizable, but provide insight into state and local perspectives.
For more information, contact Rebecca Gambler at (202) 512-8777 or gamblerr@gao.gov (mailto:gamblerr@gao.gov).

Campaign finance is the raising and spending of money to influence
electoral campaigns at the federal, state, and local levels. While most
electoral campaigns are privately financed, 14 states and 26 localities
have implemented programs that offer public financing to candidates
running for certain state and local offices, such as governor, state
representative, mayor, or county council, as of 2024.1 At the federal level,
public financing of political campaigns is available to presidential
campaigns, but has not been widely used by major party candidates since
the 2008 election.
Supporters of public financing of political campaigns see these programs
as a way to increase competition, while reducing the influence of private
money in the political process and enabling candidates to spend more
time connecting with citizens rather than raising campaign funds.
Opponents of these programs believe that they restrict free speech
because they may limit the amount of money that candidates can spend
on political advertisements, and they may force taxpayers to subsidize
candidates whose views they may oppose.

Campaign finance refers to the raising and spending of money to
influence electoral campaigns. Money raised for an electoral campaign is
also referred to as a campaign “donation” or “contribution,” and money
spent on a campaign is referred to as a campaign “expenditure.” Most
expenditures on elections are privately financed, via contributions from
individuals, political committees, and other organizations such as
corporations, unions, and tax-exempt organizations.6 In addition to these
private sources of funding, federal public campaign financing is available
for qualifying candidates for President of the United States during both
the primaries and the general election, and in states and localities that
have implemented their own public campaign financing programs.
States and localities that have implemented public campaign financing
programs have generally used three different models, according to our
review of relevant literature and interviews with representatives from
organizations familiar with these programs:
• Grants. The jurisdiction provides qualifying candidates with lump-sum
grants of public funds to finance their campaigns. The grant amount can
be either for the full or partial cost of a campaign, depending on the
program. In full grant systems, also called “clean elections” programs,
participating candidates may only make campaign expenditures with
public funds and may not raise private contributions after receipt of the
grant.
• Matching Funds. The jurisdiction matches certain private contributions
received by participating candidates with public funds at a set rate.
Depending on the jurisdiction, private contributions are matched either
dollar for dollar or at some multiple of public-to-private dollars. Generally,

categories. These four categories are (1) program goals, (2) program
funding and revenue sources, (3) candidate qualification and participation
requirements, and (4) oversight mechanisms to ensure program integrity.

In summary
Prop. 4 would lift a ban that prohibits state and most local candidates from using public funding for their political campaigns. Proponents argue the mechanism helps more candidates run for office, but opponents are skeptical.

In 1988, a Democrat, a Republican and an independent in the state Legislature co-authored a ballot measure to ban most political campaigns from using public money.
Their rationale? There was already too much money in politics.
“It certainly makes no sense to open the biggest money source of all, the taxpayers’ purses and wallets,” proponents argued (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1988&context=ca_ballot_props). Nearly 60% of voters agreed.
Almost four decades later, some good-government groups argue that the state needs to do the exact opposite to counter the influence of money in politics.
They, along with the state Democratic Party, are backing Proposition 4 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-4-public-fundraising/) on the November ballot, which would lift the 1988 ban and authorize the state and most local governments to set up public campaign financing systems for state and local races.
Seven charter cities in California, including San Francisco, Berkeley and Oakland, were spared from the 1988 ban and already have public campaign financing.
To qualify for the funding, candidates must meet criteria such as proving they have a certain number of small donors or agreeing to cap how much they raise and spend on their campaign. Depending on the city, eligible candidates receive the funding as a grant, a matching fund indexed to their total donations, or a voucher voters can give to campaigns.
Proponents of Prop. 4 may face an uphill battle: Voters have twice rejected similar ballot measures to lift the ban, and public polling so far suggests voters are skeptical.
What supporters, opponents say
Elections have gotten more expensive over the past three decades, both federally and statewide.
In 2000, federal candidates, parties and special interests spent $5.6 billion on congressional and presidential races. By 2020, that number had nearly quadrupled to $18 billion (https://www.opensecrets.org/elections-overview/cost-of-election?display=T), according to OpenSecrets, a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit that tracks campaign spending nationwide.
In California, special interests spent $26 million (https://calmatters.org/politics/2025/10/prop50-money-ads-mailers-billboards/) running competing ads on redistricting last year, making it the most expensive ballot measure race in state history. This year, California had the most expensive governor’s race (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/03/us/elections/california-governor-campaign-finance.html) in U.S. history, with billionaire Tom Steyer pouring $213 million (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-rich-candidates-funding-elections/) of his own money into his unsuccessful gubernatorial bid.
Supporters of Prop. 4 say public campaign financing is necessary as a check against that kind of unfettered private campaign spending, because candidates often must accept campaign spending limits to qualify for public funding. They say public financing will lead to more diverse candidates by attracting those who otherwise couldn’t afford to run for office.
